newsitem.title: INDIA: India cites six aircraft near-misses since Nov.
newsitem.headline: India cites six aircraft near-misses since Nov.

text.p: There have been six near-misses over Indian skies in the three months since the world's worst mid-air collision near Delhi in November, Civil Aviation Minister C.M. Ibrahim said on Tuesday.

Ibrahim said in a written statement to the Rajya Sabha, the upper house of parliament, that the government was modernising air-traffic services and insisting on proper maintenance of communication equipment and training of professionals to avoid further mid-air collisions.

But he said there had been six close calls since a Saudi Arabia Airlines Boeing 747 and a Kazakh Ilyushin Il-76 freighter collided about 80 km (50 miles) west of New Delhi on November 12, killing all 349 people aboard the two aircraft.

Ibrahim said Dutch airline KLM flight KLM 807 and Emirates Airlines flight UAE 082 nearly collided on November 16, and there were another five near-misses in January, two of them involving foreign airlines.

Kuwait Airways' flight KAC 365 and Air Lanka's flight ALK 505 nearly collided on January 11, Ibrahim's statement said, while Malaysian Airlines flight MAS 6125 and Singapore Airlines flight SIA 422 were involved in a near-miss on January 17.
The three other near-misses in the period involved Indian passenger planes.
The mid-air collision in November focused world attention on flight safety in India, where economic growth has spurred tourism, putting pressure on outdated air-traffic systems.
A multi-million-dollar plan to modernise radar and communications systems at major airports has fallen well behind schedule.

Due to go into operation six months ago, a state-of-the-art air traffic control system built by Raytheon Co of the United States has been held up by technical glitches. In November, Raytheon had said the system would soon be ready for use.
India needs huge doses of private investment to build vital airport infrastructure and spruce up flight safety, aviation experts say.
India dismantled a state aviation monopoly as part of a series of sweeping economic reforms in 1991, opening its skies to a dozen private airlines.

Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's cabinet in January allowed foreign investors to take stakes of up to 40 percent in domestic airlines but said foreign airlines could not directly buy stakes in domestic airlines.
India has five international and 87 domestic airports. The Delhi and Bombay airports handle nearly half the total traffic.
Indian airports handled some 23 million passengers in 1993. That figure is estimated to rise to 110 million by the year 2011.
